Mother Dairy passes on 75-80 per cent of its milk sales realisation to farmers.

articles.title: IndiGo extends Saudi Arabia flight suspensions to Jeddah, Madinah, Riyadh and Dammam
articles.summary: IndiGo has extended the suspension of commercial flights to four destinations in Saudi Arabia amid continuing safety and security concerns, with services to Jeddah and Madinah halted until November 21 and those to Riyadh and Dammam suspended until November 30, 2026.The airline announced the extension in a travel advisory on social media platform X on November 10, stating that the decision followed a review of the prevailing security situation."Following a careful assessment of the safety and security considerations, IndiGo has further extended the suspension of flights to and from Jeddah and Madinah until 21 November 2026 (inclusive), and Riyadh and Dammam until 30 November 2026 (inclusive)," the airline announced in its advisory.IndiGo said it was contacting affected passengers through the details provided during booking. Customers are being informed about ticket re-accommodation, refunds and alternative travel arrangements."Timely notifications are being sent to affected customers using the contact details provided at the time of booking. We remain committed to keeping our customers informed and extending the necessary assistance during this period," the airline said.— IndiGo6E (@IndiGo6E) Reiterating its position on passenger and crew safety, the airline added, "The safety and security of our customers and crew remain our highest priority. We continue to closely monitor the situation and will share further updates as necessary."The extension comes amid renewed hostilities between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthi rebels following the breakdown of a 2022 truce that had paused fighting in the country's prolonged civil war. The Houthis have previously targeted Saudi airports, energy infrastructure and military installations.On November 8, Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Energy confirmed that an administrative building belonging to Saudi Aramco in Riyadh had been targeted in an attempted attack.An official source at the ministry said falling shrapnel caused minor damage to the building. Iran crisis fuels a crude war in Myanmar
articles.summary: Myaing, Myanmar: Myanmar's small-scale oil prospectors are under fire from all sides as rebels and the military battle to capture a cottage industry increasingly lucrative amidst the Middle East energy shock."As long as we work here, bad luck can kill us," said Htun Aung, a worker on an artisanal oil well in Myanmar's arid heartlands.Also read | Jensen Huang case: Nvidia CEO love affair scandal revives push for tougher US line on China"But if the reality of death is hard to face, then making a living is even harder," said the 52-year-old, speaking under a pseudonym for security reasons.Myanmar imports 90 percent of its fuel oil, official figures show, making it particularly vulnerable to supply issues caused by the US-Israeli war on Iran.But the central region of Magway hosts a hardscrabble industry of domestic prospectors manning grimy derricks that squelch up crude oil in humble quantities.The area is dubbed "Anyar Dubai", associating the Anyar landscape with the oil boom Emirate, despite the pitiable $50 per week earned by workers like Htun Aung who spend their days drenched in foul crude run-off.With prices at Myanmar's petrol pumps nearly double what they were in late February, the underground "black gold" is an increasingly coveted prize of war.Also read | Trump's Iran war may be 'militarily' over, but economic siege still haunts"We just want to live in peace," said Htun Aung. "But now they strike from one side and the others strike from the other -- they keep attacking each other.""We've had to flee three, four, five times already," he added. "We run here, we run there. We fill up our motorbikes with fuel and run again."Digging inAllied pro-democracy rebels claim to have controlled oil fields in Magway's Myaing township since 2023, the third year of a nationwide civil war triggered by a coup.They patrol the dusty territory in a westward crook of the Irrawaddy river in ragtag columns and outfitted with rocket-propelled grenades, flak jackets, tote bags and flip-flops.Air and drone strikes in Myaing so far this year have already exceeded 2025's total, according to ACLED, a monitor that estimates more than 100,000 people have died since the putsch.Rebels shelter in foxholes, camouflaged among thousands of oil wells dug in an unregulated practice dating back centuries.Engine winches chug day and night, plunging plumbing tubes dozens of metres down boreholes before dragging them up filled with crude oil slurry.Prospectors pay landowners up to $3,500 to lease a spot to drill,one veteran said, with no guarantee they will hit oil.Some wells yield dribbles while others gush profit, filling tarpaulin-lined pits and barrels with oil hauled off to improvised refineries for processing into petrol and diesel."Anyar Dubai" has been "going viral" for its plentiful supply, said rebel spokesman Pyae Phyo Kyaw, at a time when Myanmar military-held areas have been rationing petrol.He touted recent offensives fending off military advances, but admitted being battered by counter-attacks."We see it primarily as an attempt to destroy what has been a strong supply route and source of revenue for us," said the 35-year-old, speaking under his real name.Myanmar's military could not be reached for comment.But in September, a month-long military operation claimed to have captured over 130 wells in Myaing and 735 more in neighbouring Pakokku township.Black marketScores of pro-democracy factions and ethnic minority armed groups are fighting the military over the 2021 coup that ousted the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi.As the war grinds on, all sides battle to fill war chests with the tax or trade of natural resources: gem mines, rare earth mineral deposits, gold or teak.Oil projects are not generally contested.The major ones are under staunch military guard, and on-the-books output is tiny by international standards -- around 6,000 barrels a day last year, according to the US Energy Information Administration.But artisanal fields are coveted by rebels precisely because of their modest size, according to Thomas Kean, senior Myanmar consultant for the International Crisis Group."Part of the reason why they're significant is because they're not globally significant," he said, explaining that they are small enough to thrive under the radar, yet big enough to fund guerrillas.Spiking oil prices may not directly drive conflict, said Kean, highlighting a broader military campaign to evict rebels from heartland footholds by squeezing revenue sources.But as the spoils of war become more profitable, the stakes get higher."We're talking about millions of barrels a year coming out of these oil fields," he added."With global prices what they are, that's a significant amount of money."

articles.title: US: Hegseth impeachment bid gets blocked
articles.summary: WASHINGTON: The House on Tuesday turned aside a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, halting an effort to remove the Pentagon chief for his conduct in office and his handling of the war in Iran.The vote came as Republicans grapple with the fallout from sweeping midterm losses that some in the party have blamed on the war in Iran and the resulting surge in gas prices. But after President Donald Trump signaled strong support for Hegseth, GOP lawmakers largely stood by the secretary Tuesday. They rejected the impeachment effort led by Kentucky Republican Thomas Massie and backed by Democrats.Also read | UN body agrees to postpone review of US rights record after Trump administration snubThe vote may only delay an impeachment push against Hegseth, with Democrats set to take control of the House and Senate in January.House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become the next speaker when Democrats take charge in January, stood firmly behind the push, saying Hegseth has "abused his power" and "undermined America's national security."Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer endorsed Hegseth's impeachment as well.Hegseth rebuked the effort Tuesday in his first news conference in months, portraying Massie as a rogue lawmaker and arguing he had committed none of the high crimes required in the Constitution for his removal. He framed the effort as an indictment against the nation's service members and their successes and said it was undermining American forces "in real time.""This is not patriotism," Hegseth said. Fed’s Christopher Waller opens door to 50-basis-point December rate hike after hot CPI
articles.summary: Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller's remarks intensified the debate over a possible half-percentage-point interest-rate increase in December after US inflation data came in hotter than expected on Tuesday, Bloomberg reported.In a speech delivered in London before the release of October’s Consumer Price Index, Waller said he was inclined to support a rate increase in December. He warned that a 50-basis-point move might be necessary if inflation continued to accelerate, arguing that the Fed’s credibility could otherwise be at risk.Hours later, data showed that consumer prices rose more than expected. Core inflation, which excludes food and energy, increased 0.3% from the previous month, meeting the threshold Waller identified as grounds for considering a larger rate increase.Also read: Traders raise odds of 50 bps Fed rate hike as CPI rise exceeds expectationsWaller’s remarks represent the clearest signal yet from a Fed official that policymakers may need to raise rates in December by more than the quarter-percentage-point move markets had expected.Several senior Fed officials, including Vice Chair Philip Jefferson and New York Fed President John Williams, are scheduled to speak this week.Fed watchers said Waller’s comments did not make a 50-basis-point move certain but would add urgency to the debate over how aggressively policymakers must act to contain inflation.“This is not a print that screams out the need to go 50, but certainly provides ammunition to the argument to do so,” Christopher Hodge, chief US economist at Natixis, told Bloomberg.For live updates on US Markets, click hereTom Porcelli, chief economist at Wells Fargo, said he expected the Fed’s policy-setting committee to support another rate increase unanimously, although the size of the move remained open for debate.“This locks it down,” Porcelli said, referring to the likelihood of at least a 25-basis-point increase. “With Waller introducing that idea, the market is going to run with it in the face of this firm print.”Following Waller’s remarks and the inflation report, investors priced in a more aggressive path for interest rates in the coming months. However, markets remained unconvinced that policymakers would deliver a half-point increase in December.Federal funds futures continued to indicate a quarter-point move in December, followed by additional increases of the same size in January and possibly April. Investors had previously expected rate increases in December and March.Waller described the US economy as strong and the labour market as stable but said inflation remained too high.“If, as I expect, the monthly rate of inflation improves in October, I am leaning toward supporting an increase in our policy rate of 25 basis points,” Waller said.“But if the October CPI inflation data out later today are similar to the past two monthly readings—with core CPI inflation around 0.3% or even higher—then a stronger policy move may be needed,” he added. “In that case, I believe a 50 basis point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting.”Under such a scenario, Waller said a conventional quarter-point increase would do little to reassure the public that the Fed was serious about controlling inflation.“Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take,” he said.Also Read: Are days of easy money over? Aswath Damodaran warns of a new mkt realityHot CPI intensifies rate debateData released later by the Bureau of Labor Statistics showed that core consumer prices rose 0.3% in October from the previous month, while the headline CPI increased 0.4%.Fed officials held interest rates steady last month, saying the “accumulation of more information” would help them determine the appropriate policy setting.The 10-2 decision followed a unanimous vote in September to raise the benchmark rate by 25 basis points to a target range of 3.75% to 4%. Several policymakers have since indicated that additional increases may be necessary.Data released last week showed that job growth accelerated in October while the unemployment rate edged lower. Fed officials will receive another employment report and a full set of inflation data before their December meeting.During a question-and-answer session with Bloomberg’s Francine Lacqua after the speech, Waller said the Fed did not want to “slam the economy down.”“It’s not that we’re going to jack up the policy rate 150 basis points or 200 basis points,” he said. “We are looking forward and saying we need to do something; at a minimum, probably take back the three insurance cuts that we put in last year.”Waller added that monetary policy had not been “nearly as restrictive as I thought it was.”(Disclaimer: This article is based on inputs from agencies. These do not represent the views of The Economic Times)

articles.title: Rupee set for another winning run?
articles.summary: The Indian rupee may appreciate further against the US dollar over the next couple of months, supported by easing global headwinds, declining crude oil prices, improving foreign capital inflows and a weakening US dollar, according to economists.Speaking to ANI, former UN adviser and economist Santosh Mehrotra said the domestic currency could strengthen further if the recent easing of global economic and geopolitical pressures continues."Overall, we can expect the Indian rupee to appreciate further over the coming couple of months," Mehrotra said, adding that the outlook would depend on whether global headwinds, which are currently subsiding, remain subdued or ease further.Explaining the factors behind the rupee's recent strengthening, Mehrotra said the Democrats' victory in both chambers of the US Congress had weakened the dollar by reducing the political and fiscal risk premium associated with the currency.He noted that the election outcome could make it more difficult for US President Donald Trump to push through his fiscal and spending agenda, potentially limiting fiscal expansion.Mehrotra also pointed to the possibility of de-escalation in the Middle East, which could reduce geopolitical risks and ease the risk premium in international crude oil prices.He said international crude prices, which were around USD 105 per barrel before the US election results, had declined to approximately USD 96 per barrel.With India importing around 90 per cent of its crude oil requirements, lower international oil prices could reduce the country's import bill and provide support to the domestic currency.Mehrotra also highlighted the return of foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) to Indian equity markets as another factor supporting the rupee.He said foreign investors had purchased approximately USD 1 billion worth of Indian equities in November up to November 5, contributing to dollar inflows into the country.Additionally, he noted that the unwinding of investments in artificial intelligence-related stocks and technology companies in the US and North Asian economies could redirect capital towards other emerging markets, including India.Another supporting factor, according to Mehrotra, was the decline in US Treasury yields.He said US bond yields had eased from around 5.3 per cent to 5.2 per cent on the first day following the election results, as investors anticipated that a Democrat-controlled Congress could constrain Trump's fiscal expansion plans.Lower US Treasury yields could reduce the relative attractiveness of dollar-denominated assets and encourage investors to explore emerging-market bonds offering higher returns.Mehrotra added that Indian government securities had also benefited from improving market conditions, with yields declining by 11 basis points in November.Meanwhile, Devendra Pant, Chief Economist at India Ratings and Research Private Limited, told that declining crude oil prices, a narrowing gap between petroleum product and food prices, and the possibility of lower freight rates could further support the rupee.Pant said freight rates could ease if the announcement of no further US military activity in the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding areas translated into a sustained reduction in regional tensions.He noted that these developments, alongside measures taken by the government and the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to improve dollar availability, could help stabilise the domestic currency.These measures included the RBI directly providing dollars to oil marketing companies, reducing their need to purchase dollars from the market, along with measures relating to gold.Pant further highlighted that lower crude oil prices could moderate gas prices and ease pressure on the government's fertiliser subsidy bill, a major expenditure component that could otherwise affect fiscal calculations.He added that declining oil prices would also reduce the cost of petroleum imports compared with expectations prevailing a week or 10 days earlier.According to Pant, these developments could result in a lower-than-anticipated current account deficit, while capital inflows, particularly foreign portfolio investments, could improve.Asked about the extent of potential rupee appreciation, Pant said it was difficult to predict a specific level, although the overall outlook remained positive."I will not stick my neck out to give a number. The outlook is, you can say cautious optimism, and the rupee is likely to strengthen further," he said.However, Pant cautioned that any adverse geopolitical developments could reverse the currency's strengthening trend.He said that if the temporary truce or peace in the region holds, the rupee could appreciate further. Even in the event of depreciation, he expected the movement to remain orderly rather than witnessing the sharp declines seen over the past year or year and a half.Pant added that the global economic environment was showing signs of improvement, with headwinds originating in the Middle East gradually easing, a development that could benefit India's economy and international trade.

articles.title: India's water journey a model: WB official
articles.summary: United Nations: From bringing drinking water to millions of households to cleaning one of its most revered rivers, India's efforts to address its water challenges are increasingly drawing attention beyond its borders, with a senior World Bank official describing the initiatives as a model for developing nations."For the World Bank Group, India is a remarkable success story. It's the water journey that every single developing country is looking at," Saroj Kumar Jha, Global Director for Water at the World Bank Group, said in response to a PTI question during a virtual press briefing ahead of the 2026 United Nations Water Conference.Also Read: 2026 set to rank among four warmest years on record, says WMOThe recognition comes at a time when water security is increasingly becoming a global development priority, with countries grappling with the twin challenges of ensuring equitable access to clean water and protecting existing water resources from pollution and unsustainable use.Co-hosted by the United Arab Emirates and Senegal, the UN Water Conference will be held in Abu Dhabi from December 8 to 10.It will bring together world leaders, policymakers and other stakeholders to explore ways to strengthen international cooperation on water security and sanitation.Also Read: As Delhi gasps for clean air, parliamentary panel skips hearing on air pollutionFor Jha, India's experience offers something beyond ambitious targets and large-scale government programmes, a practical blueprint that other developing nations can adapt to their own circumstances.He highlighted several Indian initiatives, including the Jal Jeevan Mission, Namami Gange and Swachh Bharat Mission.Jha said during his recent visit to New Delhi and meetings with Indian government officials, he had encouraged them to use the international conference as a platform to share its experience and demonstrate how large-scale water management initiatives could be implemented."India has done what other countries are now trying to work on, and India offers the how-to part of the water solution," he said.Among the initiatives that have particularly impressed the World Bank is the Jal Jeevan Mission, which has sought to transform access to drinking water in rural India.Highlighting the scale of the programme, Jha said reaching 800 million people with improved drinking water access in less than seven years is a "remarkable" achievement.He described India's efforts to expand drinking water access in both urban and rural areas as "unprecedented", while pointing out that the programme is now evolving beyond expanding coverage to focus increasingly on sustainability, operations and maintenance.India's sanitation experience, too, has found resonance abroad. Jha cited Nigeria's 'Clean Nigeria' campaign as an initiative influenced by India's Swachh Bharat Mission."What India has done is already spreading to many other countries across the globe, and particularly countries in the South are looking at Jal Jeevan Mission as a good model to replicate with popular participation of people, government-strong leadership, adequate financing at all levels," he said.If access to drinking water and sanitation represents one dimension of India's water transformation, the effort to restore the health of its rivers represents another.Jha described the Namami Gange Programme as "remarkably successful" in reducing pollution in the Ganga and improving the overall health of the river.The World Bank has supported the National Mission for Clean Ganga through various financing instruments.For Jha, river conservation also has a significance that goes well beyond environmental protection."Rivers are not just rivers; they are part of our civilisation, part of the human system. People depend on these rivers for their livelihood," he said.The World Bank official also highlighted India's efforts to improve dam safety, saying the bank's funding had helped strengthen the resilience of nearly 900 dams. The establishment of centres of excellence has further helped build technical expertise and institutional capacity in the sector.India's urban water management initiatives also drew praise, particularly efforts to encourage creditworthy municipalities to tap capital markets and mobilise resources for improving civic water services.Jha acknowledged that India continued to face considerable challenges in water management, but said the progress made at both the central and state levels offered valuable lessons for other countries."We are looking at the entire system of water management in India... What they have done in this field is really remarkable, at the state level and the central government level," he said.India is expected to play an active role in the upcoming UN conference.Stephanie Rambler, Senior Sustainable Development Officer at the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs, said the country is "very active" in preparations.India is expected to send a large high-level government delegation and organise a side event on 'river cities', focusing on water security and resilience, she said.The conference will feature seven plenary meetings and six interactive dialogues, besides special events aimed at accelerating progress towards Sustainable Development Goal 6, which seeks to ensure access to clean water and sanitation for all.

Russia, Ukraine first peace talks in 9 mths
articles.summary: Abu Dhabi: Russian and Ukrainian officials met in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday for their first US-brokered talks since February, after President Donald Trump suggested last week that a broad deal was possible on ending the war in Ukraine and guaranteeing security in Europe.US envoy Jared Kushner told delegates that recent contacts with both sides had "really identified, narrowed the gaps", and the US side had "some good ideas" on how to bridge their differences. Trump, he said, was committed to achieving peace.Also Read: US-mediated talks on ending Russia-Ukraine war begin in Abu Dhabi"He really has asked us to put extra effort into trying to find a solution that hopefully ends the war but also leaves both sides in a much stronger position" to realise their full potential, Kushner said.But more than 4-1/2 years after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and with Russian forces holding about a fifth of the country, Moscow and Kyiv remain far apart - despite Trump's optimism - on terms for a possible settlement.Ukraine's chief delegate, Rustem Umerov, said in his opening remarks that Kyiv was focused on achieving security guarantees and a lasting peace.Also Read: Trump says Iran war's 'militarily' over, but US 'locked and loaded'Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov underlined Moscow's preference for negotiating a broad European security framework before tackling the specifics of the war."The idea of ​​defining clear parameters for a future security architecture, and only then moving on to resolving the actual Russia-Ukraine conflict, is absolutely reasonable," he told reporters in Moscow.European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Monday voiced the opposite view, saying wider security talks should come only after a ceasefire in Ukraine. Lavrov again rejected the notion of a truce, saying the Europeans were trying to buy breathing space for Ukraine.Europeans seek a role in the processThe new American drive for a deal has galvanized European officials into pushing for a place at the table to seek an end to the continent's deadliest conflict since World War Two.Before the start of the main meeting, the Ukrainians met separately with European, NATO and EU representatives and the two American envoys, Kushner and Steve Witkoff.France said there could be no lasting peace in Ukraine without addressing European security, and that this required the involvement of the Europeans.Russia had made clear it did not see a place for Europeans at the meeting with the Ukrainians and Americans.On the eve of the talks, Trump said Washington was seeing a "very strong inclination" towards ending the war, and that both sides were "tired of fighting". After meeting privately with Russian President Vladimir Putin's envoy last week at the White House, Trump predicted that a peace deal could emerge soon.Trump has frequently said an agreement was close, without a deal emerging. However, negotiations have picked up again in recent weeks after months in which Washington's attention was focused on the war in Iran.Publicly, there has been no sign that Putin is willing to drop his insistence that Ukraine surrender the entire eastern region of Donbas before a peace deal can be struck.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy has refused to hand over land that his forces have died defending.Russian front-line advances have slowed to a virtual halt this year but Moscow has been pounding Ukrainian cities and energy facilities, while Ukraine has stepped up attacks on oil refineries and other infrastructure deep inside Russia.A source in the Russian delegation said Russia believed the main thrust of the talks would be trying to hammer out the key elements of a new post-war security framework for Europe.On the eve of the negotiations, Zelenskiy said Ukraine's leverage in the talks was increasing as a result of its recent battlefield performance, which has included retaking some territory in Donetsk, a coal-mining area of the Donbas."Ukrainian forces are currently genuinely strengthening Ukraine's negotiating position," Zelenskiy said in his nightly video address on Monday. He said Russia was suffering "record losses" - an assertion disputed by Moscow - and urged Washington to convince the Kremlin to end the war.US negotiators believe that Zelenskiy and Putin may be willing to strike a compromise on the vital question of territory, each ceding a little, a US official told Reuters.Under the proposed deal, Ukraine would get an end to the war, security guarantees and a roadmap to accession to the EU.A senior Ukrainian official strongly denied that the government would consider any such concessions. The issue of territory could be discussed only at the leaders' level and only in the context of appropriate security guarantees for Ukraine, the official said.

Nvidia board faces 'honey pot' test
articles.summary: Revelations that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a businesswoman suspected of being a Chinese spy have forced the chipmaker's board to confront more than ordinary executive misconduct, raising existential questions for the company and concerns about the board's ability to investigate its CEO independently.Among corporate leaders, "There have definitely been affair scandals and sexual-harassment scandals. But honey-pot scandals? No," said Ann Lipton, a University of Colorado law professor who follows boardroom issues.She was using a term for an espionage ploy in which an operative entraps a target by feigning romantic interest. Historical examples include the Profumo Affair in the early 1960s and tend to involve diplomatic or political consequences.Also Read: Jensen Huang's price of secret affair: NVIDIA CEO loses $7.4 billion in 30 minutes, drops 2 spots in top 10 richest listUS President Donald Trump said on Monday the FBI was probing Huang's relationship, a day after Nvidia's board launched an internal investigation "regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports," according to an email Huang sent to Nvidia employees and released by the company.The company's advanced semiconductors are at the heart of a global race for AI superiority. China's Foreign Ministry said the spying claim was "a groundless accusation, slander, and a smear."Nvidia co-founder Huang, 63, has no obvious successor and close ties to Trump. He owns 3.6% of its stock and has dozens of direct reports, suggesting a tight grip on the company.Shares in Nvidia fell Monday as Huang's future came under scrutiny. But the stock later trimmed its decline to close 4% lower as some investors bet that the CEO could survive the crisis.BOARD'S CREDIBILITYUnusually among its peers, Nvidia operates without a board chair among its 11 directors. While the company considers all but Huang independent, three independent directors have served since the 1990s and a fourth, Mark Stevens, for most of that time. Only two have joined the board since 2021.The clubby roster may not be so unusual by the standards of charismatic Silicon Valley company founders like Apple's Steve Jobs, who died in 2011.But the US probe has heightened scrutiny of whether directors who have worked alongside Huang for decades are sufficiently independent to investigate his conduct."If you have a figure like Steve Jobs, I think people on Wall Street as well as in Silicon Valley would say they're entitled to some leeway or deference," said Marc Goldstein, head of US research for proxy adviser Institutional Shareholder Services.Such deference could now raise questions about whether the board provided sufficient oversight of a CEO whose own judgment has come under scrutiny.Nvidia said on Sunday that while its board had no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, its inquiry would examine ​all available information. The board said it had confidence in the CEO and his leadership team.Goldstein said board members running that investigation should be given the latitude to hire their own legal advisers to bolster their credibility.The company also might consider keeping long-serving directors away from the probe, he added, to avoid legal challenges from shareholders claiming it wasn't sufficiently independent.POLITICAL ECONOMYYale University management professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld said the company faces additional national-security questions because of the ties between Huang and Trump. Trump, who has praised Huang, said on Monday that he had spoken to the executive and thought he would "be in good shape."Washington has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China since ​2022. Last year the Trump administration allowed Nvidia to resume certain China shipments under arrangements in which the US government receives a cut of the company's China chip sales.The deal makes any suggestion of foreign espionage more sensitive for both executives and US government officials, Sonnenfeld said. "That's why you don't want state capitalism arrangements. You don't want the US government to be so involved in private companies," he said.

Warren Buffett’s 7 golden rules for young investors trying to manage finances
articles.summary: Young investors often find it difficult to manage their finances as rising number of responsibilities and expenses take a toll on savings. But billionaire and market veteran Warren Buffett has some advice for them.Buffett took control of a struggling textile company at the age of 35 in 1965 and transformed it into Berkshire Hathaway, now valued at more than $1 trillion, with annual after-tax operating earnings of about $45 billion. Buffett handed over the CEO role to longtime deputy Greg Abel this year, and recently passed on the Chairman role to his son, Howard Buffett.The 96-year-old Warren Buffett, even after retirement, continues to inspire generations to come. Here are pieces of his advice that can help young investors.1) Live below your meansWarren Buffett once famously treated fellow billionaire and Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates not at a fancy restaurant, but at his favourite McDonald’s, and that too using coupons. This famously simple act speaks volumes about the market veteran’s frugal lifestyle.He lives in the Omaha house he bought for $31,500 in 1958. The five-bedroom home is now worth about $1.3 million, but Buffett says he would never trade it because it holds memories of raising his three children. He also avoids splurging on expensive cars. The legendary investor drives a 2014 Cadillac XTS, complete with hail damage, because, in his words, giving up half a day to shop for a new car isn’t worth it. He even once had a license plate that read “THRIFTY,” a fitting symbol for one of the world’s richest individuals who chooses to live simply.Also read | Warren Buffett’s 6 golden rules for investors after retirement“I do not think that standard of living equates with cost of living beyond a certain point,” Buffett said at a Berkshire Hathaway shareholders meeting in 2014. “My life would not be happier: it would be worse if I had six or eight houses or a whole bunch of different things I could have. It just doesn’t correlate.” Whether it’s mansions or sports cars, Buffett avoids major purchases that reflect his wealth, believing they may ultimately detract from his happiness.2) Pay off high-interest debt as soon as possibleWarren Buffett also strongly advised people to pay off any high-interest debt they may have, like credit card debt. In fact, the ace investor believes that paying off your credit card debt is one of the best guaranteed ways to get a return on your money.If you are drowning in debt, work out a payment plan to pay back your creditors as soon as possible, or the interest will keep piling up. After you're debt-free, make it a point to set aside funds for investments from your income regularly.3) Think long-term while investingThe legendary investor advocated for long-term investing and not short-term quick trades. Buffett has famously said, "Our favourite holding period is forever." His long-term holdings have included Coca-Cola, American Express and Wells Fargo.By emphasising low costs, diversification, and long-term growth, Buffett’s rule continues to gain attention as a reliable strategy for everyday Americans seeking financial security.Also read | Michael Burry's top 10 life lessons for GenZ: 'Buy half the house you can afford'4) Invest in what you knowWarren Buffett has repeatedly stressed the importance of staying within one's "circle of competence." "You only have to be able to evaluate companies within your circle of competence. The size of that circle is not very important; knowing its boundaries, however, is vital."Buffett famously avoided technology stocks during the dot-com boom of the late 1990s because he believed forecasting the long-term survival of young technology companies was outside his expertise.5) Always have a cash reserveWhile Warren Buffett is a bullish stock market investor, he did encourage people to hold some amount of cash reserves. “You do need oxygen, and if you are ever without it for four or five minutes, you will learn. And cash is that way. So you always need to have it available, because you do not know what will happen,” Buffett told CNBC during an interview earlier this year. He, however, added that while holding cash at certain levels is necessary, it is not a good asset.The legendary investor likes to keep some level of cash to pay obligations and as “dry powder” for any attractive acquisitions.Also read | Peter Lynch on stock picking: 'You shouldn't own a stock if you can't…'6) The 90/10 investment ruleIn his 2013 letter to Berkshire Hathaway shareholders, Warren Buffett introduced his 90/10 investment rule by sharing what he wrote in part of his will. With reference to a cash inheritance going to his wife, he advised his will's trustee to keep 90% of the cash inheritance in an S&P 500 index fund and 10% in short-term government bonds. Buffett believed this mix offers the best balance of growth and stability for non-professional investors. The S&P 500 provides exposure to America’s largest and most profitable companies, while Treasury bonds act as a cushion during market downturns.7) Remember that money isn’t everythingBuffett is among the richest people in the world, but he does not use this metric as a measure of success. “Being given unconditional love is the greatest benefit you can ever get,” he told MBA students in a 2008 talk.“The incredible thing about love is that you can’t get rid of it. If you try to give it away, you end up with twice as much, but if you try to hold onto it, it disappears. articles.title: Is AI selloff a window to buy? Morgan Stanley sees multiple buying opportunities on Wall Street
articles.summary: As the frenzy around artificial intelligence (AI) fizzles out, Morgan Stanley has struck a positive note, with the international brokerage firm seeing buying opportunities among AI enablers, infrastructure providers and adopters.After Democratic victories in the US midterm elections triggered concerns that a Democrat-controlled Congress would curb excessive AI spending on data centres, tech stocks plunged and have been trading on a seesaw since then. Morgan Stanley noted that Wall Street had undergone an earthquake event over the past week, with significant uncertainty surrounding the impact of the midterms on the data centre build-out, the trajectory of the cycle and the implications for global stocks.It broadly views the recent market weakness as unwarranted. “We see the market moves as an overreaction and think the ultimate impact will be a push-out of some projects from 2028 to 2029, rather than a derailing of the capex story. This has the potential to elongate the AI capex cycle, which has positives including a smoother supply-demand rebalancing across the data centre supply chain, improved credit outlook, and higher lease rates for compute,” it said.Also read | Anthropic retracts details of $69 billion IPO filing sent to bankers. Why analysts are raising worries over valuationsMorgan Stanley has sized the impact on the data centre build-out and flagged implications for stocks, policy and equity strategy across the US, Asia and Europe. "We are recommending a selective ‘Buy the Drop’ strategy and remain most constructive on the hyperscalers, select semis/infrastructure/time-to-power solutions that have de-rated materially, and software enablers and AI adopters as AI value creation broadens,” it further said.How Trump's midterm defeat can impact the AI tradeThe newly elected Democratic governors are unlikely to disrupt projects under construction, leaving 2027 projects unchanged, Morgan Stanley said. However, it believes some 2028 projects in Texas and Ohio will be delayed to 2029, as governors work with legislators to put in place new requirements for data centre developers.The international research firm shifted 5 GW of US data centre capacity from 2028 to 2029, representing 20% of US projects and 10% of global projects. This implies that US data centre capacity additions will decline 4% year-on-year in 2028 and rise 38% year-on-year in 2029. Globally, this implies data centre additions will rise 9% year-on-year in 2028 and 20% in 2029.“This could create an air-pocket across the tech supply chain in 2028, leading to a reduction in pricing power or a build of inventory, although we believe valuations are pricing this in across many names, with the key risk being the sustainability of margins. We also believe this creates an attractive opportunity to potentially build data centres abroad and forecast 20GW of potential spillover across Asia and EMEA,” it added.That said, Morgan Stanley is mindful that delays in project approvals or initiation, on top of existing constraints around labour and materials, could put downward pressure on its 2028 capex estimates and prolong the build-out and capex cycle.“We are highly focused on increased (exponential) compute efficiencies from leading labs in 2027 to allow products to scale with less compute. Compute constraints aren't new, and they may just stay around longer with further data centre delays,” it added.Finally, financing remains available, but the midterms should deepen the quality divide, Morgan Stanley said. With capex forecasts unchanged, it still expects higher AI-related debt issuance in 2027, led by hyperscalers. New construction financings and neoclouds face greater scrutiny, making tenant quality, a credible path to energisation and contractual protections increasingly important.“We see more limited exposure to new restrictions for projects already backing outstanding bonds, although execution risk remains. Slower competing development should support stabilised, cash-flowing assets, reinforcing our preference for colocation over hyperscaler data-centre ABS.”Also read | Nithin Kamath says speculative craziness brought more people into US markets: ‘Nothing expands markets like greed, FOMO’Which AI stocks to buy?Given the significant price weakness across a range of AI-related stocks following the US election results, Morgan Stanley provided its updated views on which stocks or sectors look most attractive, highlighting three key areas. It has three main buckets of investment recommendations.These include hyperscalers (Amazon, Meta, Google and Microsoft), select data centre supply chain names, and software enablers or AI adopters. Nvidia is also mentioned among the stocks, but it belongs to the semiconductor category rather than the hyperscaler category. articles.title: Ozempic, Wegovy to carry new FDA warning over rare risk of vision loss
articles.summary:
Popular weight loss drugs including Ozempic and Wegovy will carry a new warning about a possible rare side effect that can sometimes lead to permanent vision loss, US health regulators announced Monday.
The Food and Drug Administration said the risk will be added to the labeling of all GLP-1 drugs, the blockbuster medications used to treat obesity, diabetes and several other medical conditions. The class includes a dozen injectable or pill-based drugs, including widely used brands like Zepbound and Mounjaro.
The eye condition, known as non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, can cause significant vision loss. The problem, which has been reported with all GLP-1 drugs, is caused by decreased blood flow to the optic nerve, although the underlying cause isn't understood, the FDA said.
FDA scientists began looking into the problem after the publication of a 2024 medical paper tying the condition to certain patients taking semaglutide, the active drug in Eli Lilly's Ozempic.
